newsitem.title: FRANCE: French president lavishes praise on Clinton.
newsitem.headline: French president lavishes praise on Clinton.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac lavished praise on U.S. President Bill Clinton on Wednesday after the U.S. leader was re-elected and Paris foresaw a more active U.S. foreign policy up to the new millennium.

"May I say that no one is more delighted than I am," Chirac said of Clinton's triumph in a "My dear Bill" message that belied a recent record of prickly Franco-American ties on issues ranging from NATO reform to Middle East peace.

"Your presence at the White House will guarantee us an American partner who is friendly, clear-sighted, competent but also generous," Chirac, a conservative, said of Democrat Clinton's triumph over Republican Bob Dole.
In unusually effusive language, Chirac also praised Clinton's "wise statesmanship" and said: "I know that with your re-election the close relations between our two countries will become even closer."

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said Clinton was likely to turn more to foreign policy in his second term. De Charette, who once said Paris "irritated" Washington in the Middle East, predicted few changes in U.S. policy goals abroad.
"I think the American president will be one who turns more towards foreign policy in his second term than in his first, as is the tradition in the United States," he told France-Inter radio.
Chirac told Clinton: "I am glad that it falls upon you to build the bridge to the 21st century that you envision for the United States of America."

Chirac won a seven-year term in 1995, the first leader of a major democracy elected to lead his country into the new millennium. Chirac is personally strongly pro-American, speaks fluent English, once worked at a Howard Johnson's restaurant and was even briefly engaged to a Texan belle.

"Together, it will be our task to overcome the difficulties of the turn of the century, but also to prepare a peaceful future for our children. Together we must lead our societies toward the third millennium," he said.
Opinion polls in France had shown that Clinton was overwhelmingly favoured by French citizens over Dole.
Former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, a centrist who ruled from 1974-81, said Americans had essentially rewarded Clinton for an improved economy.
He played down the gushing quality of Chirac's message.
"In politics we always praise the winners. If it had been Dole elected he would have got a telegram saying 'You're friendly, clear sighted, etc'," he said.
Giscard d'Estaing predicted Washington would become more self-assured abroad and increasingly unwilling to share responsibility with its allies.
In international policy "they want to act all alone, they want to solve the problems of the Middle East, they don't accept intervention by others," he told RTL radio.
He said Washington had also sent signals it wanted to become more assertive in African policy, long a focus of French interest.

Chirac's wife Bernadette sent her own message to Washington, telling Hillary Clinton she was "delighted" at the victory and said the president had "fine qualities" and an "infinite kindness and simplicity of manner that never leave him."
